--- title: "sportsdataverse-py × Quarto — executable-docs PoC" subtitle: "Real Python output, frozen into the page at build time" author: "SportsDataverse" date: today --- ## What this page is This is a **proof-of-concept** for documenting the Python package [`sportsdataverse-py`](https://py.sportsdataverse.org) with [Quarto](https://quarto.org). The point it demonstrates is **build-time executable code cells**: every Python block below is *actually run* when the page is rendered (`quarto render`), and its output — including tidy **polars** / **pandas** DataFrames rendered as HTML tables — is frozen into the static page. No browser runtime, no serverless proxy, no "trust me, this is what it returns": the reader sees the genuine output of `sportsdataverse` against the live ESPN endpoints as of the render. Compare this side-by-side with the Docusaurus site under `docs/` — see [`README.md`](./README.md) in this folder for the full Quarto-vs-Docusaurus write-up. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 1. The package surface First, import the package and confirm the per-sport namespaces are all present. This is a stable, offline-safe call — it touches no network. ::: {#385b41fb .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") # silence the harmless numexpr/bottleneck UserWarning import sportsdataverse as sdv sports = ["nba", "wnba", "nfl", "mlb", "nhl", "mbb", "wbb", "cfb", "odds"] present = [s for s in sports if hasattr(sdv, s)] present ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['nba', 'wnba', 'nfl', 'mlb', 'nhl', 'mbb', 'wbb', 'cfb', 'odds'] ``` ::: ::: Every sport submodule resolves. Each one exposes an `espn__*` family of tidy-data loaders. For example, the NBA namespace ships these ESPN endpoints (first dozen shown): ::: {#d1a30bab .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import sportsdataverse.nba as nba nba_espn = [fn for fn in dir(nba) if fn.startswith("espn_nba_")] print(f"{len(nba_espn)} espn_nba_* callables; first 12:") nba_espn[:12] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 115 espn_nba_* callables; first 12: ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['espn_nba_award', 'espn_nba_awards', 'espn_nba_calendar', 'espn_nba_coach', 'espn_nba_coach_record', 'espn_nba_coach_season', 'espn_nba_conferences', 'espn_nba_draft', 'espn_nba_franchise', 'espn_nba_franchises', 'espn_nba_game', 'espn_nba_game_broadcasts'] ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 2. A real loader → a real DataFrame Now the headline feature. We call `espn_nba_teams()` — a stable ESPN teams endpoint — and let Quarto render the returned **polars** DataFrame as an HTML table. This is *live data captured at build time*, not a hand-maintained sample that drifts out of date. ::: {#b4b739dd .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sportsdataverse.nba import espn_nba_teams teams = espn_nba_teams() # -> polars.DataFrame teams.shape # (rows, cols) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (30, 14) ``` ::: ::: The frame is wide (logos, colors, slugs, uids…). Let's select the three columns most readers care about and show the first ten teams. Quarto renders the polars frame inline: ::: {#066daeed .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} teams.select(["team_id", "team_abbreviation", "team_display_name"]).head(10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Because the package is polars-first but pandas-friendly, the same loader can hand back a **pandas** frame with `return_as_pandas=True` — useful when the reader's downstream stack is pandas. Quarto renders pandas frames just as happily (note the `df-print: paged` styling from `_quarto.yml`): ::: {#f39a3752 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} teams_pd = espn_nba_teams(return_as_pandas=True) teams_pd[["team_id", "team_abbreviation", "team_display_name"]].head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

4 4 CHI Chicago Bulls
``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 3. A second sport, same one-liner shape The cross-league surface is uniform: `espn__teams()` returns the same tidy shape for every league. Here is the NFL equivalent — 32 teams, rendered the same way: ::: {#6eeccc4d .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sportsdataverse.nfl import espn_nfl_teams nfl_teams = espn_nfl_teams() nfl_teams.select(["team_id", "team_abbreviation", "team_display_name"]).head(8) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 4. Inline computed results in prose Quarto also supports **inline executable expressions**, so a sentence can quote a *computed* number rather than a copy-pasted one that goes stale. ::: {#33f76011 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} n_nba = espn_nba_teams().height n_nfl = espn_nfl_teams().height ``` ::: As of this render, `sportsdataverse` reports **30 NBA teams** and **32 NFL teams** from the ESPN teams endpoints — and those two numbers were computed by Python while this page was being built, not typed in by hand. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Takeaway Every table and number on this page is the *real* output of `sportsdataverse` code, executed once at build time and frozen into static HTML. There is no client-side Python, no live API call when a reader loads the page, and no manually maintained "expected output" that can silently rot. That is the core value proposition of Quarto for the SportsDataverse **Python** (and **R**) data packages. See [`README.md`](./README.md) for how this stacks up against the Docusaurus toolchain the SportsDataverse uses elsewhere.
